title: Θυσία καὶ Ἀγερμός
titleEn: The Sacrifice and the Muster — Iliad 2.369–468
about: Agamemnon answers Nestor with praise and an admission: he began the quarrel with Achilles, and if the two of them could agree, Troy would not last. He sends the army to its meal and its preparations, warning that any man who skulks by the ships will not escape the dogs and birds. The Argives roar like surf and scatter to eat and to sacrifice, each to his own god. Agamemnon kills an ox for Zeus, calls the chiefs, and prays that he may burn Priam’s house and tear Hector’s tunic on his body before the sun sets; Zeus takes the offering but does not yet grant it. After the feast Nestor urges that no time be lost, and the heralds summon the army. Athena goes through the ranks with the aegis, and the men would sooner fight than sail home. The poet compares their bronze to a forest fire seen far off and their numbers to flocks of birds, then to leaves and flowers, as they pour onto the plain of the Scamander.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed lord Agamemnon:
sentences.i: In answer lord Agamemnon said to him:
sentences.n: This is the reply-formula, the same line as 1.130, and its English is the same. ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’ is the participle of ἀπαμείβομαι, and προσέφη ‘addressed’ is the aorist of πρόσφημι. κρείων, a participle of κρείω ‘rule’ used as a title, is given as ‘lord’. Agamemnon is answering Nestor, whose speech ended at 2.368.

sentences.t: ἦ μὰν αὖτ’ ἀγορῇ νικᾷς γέρον υἷας Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l: “Truly again in assembly you surpass, old man, the sons of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: “Truly, old man, you again surpass the sons of the Achaeans in assembly.
sentences.n: Agamemnon opens by praising Nestor, with a verb that takes a person as its object. ἦ μάν is the emphatic ‘truly’, with μάν the epic form of μήν. νικᾷς is the present of νικάω, which with an accusative of persons (υἷας Ἀχαιῶν) means ‘surpass’, not ‘defeat’. ἀγορῇ is the dative of ἀγορή ‘assembly’, the place in which he surpasses them. αὖτ’ is αὖτε ‘again’, which may recall Nestor’s earlier speech in the quarrel of Book 1 (1.254–284) or simply the speech he has just made. γέρον is the vocative of γέρων ‘old man’, and υἷας is the epic accusative plural of υἱός. The opening quotation mark begins Agamemnon’s speech, which runs to 2.393.

sentences.t:
αἲ γὰρ Ζεῦ τε πάτερ καὶ Ἀθηναίη καὶ Ἄπολλον
τοιοῦτοι δέκα μοι συμφράδμονες εἶεν Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.l:
Would that — Father Zeus, and Athena, and Apollo —
such ten to me fellow-planners might be, of the Achaeans:
sentences.i: If only — Father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo — I had ten such advisers among the Achaeans:
sentences.n: αἲ γάρ opens a wish, ‘would that’, and the first line is the line that opens a wish in the Odyssey, so its English is the Odyssey’s. The wish is carried by the optative εἶεν (from εἰμί) with μοι ‘to me’: ‘might be for me’, that is, ‘I might have’. τοιοῦτοι ‘such’ means men like Nestor, who has just spoken, though Agamemnon does not name him. συμφράδμονες, from σύν ‘together’ and φράζομαι ‘plan’, are those who plan with one, ‘fellow-planners’, and Ἀχαιῶν is partitive, ‘of the Achaeans’. Ζεῦ πάτερ is a vocative, ‘Father Zeus’.

sentences.t:
τώ κε τάχ’ ἠμύσειε πόλις Πριάμοιο ἄνακτος
χερσὶν ὑφ’ ἡμετέρῃσιν ἁλοῦσά τε περθομένη τε.
sentences.l:
Then soon would the city of lord Priam bow down,
beneath our hands taken and being sacked.
sentences.i: Then the city of lord Priam would soon fall, taken and sacked beneath our hands.
sentences.n: τώ is τῷ ‘then, in that case’, the result of the wish; κε with the optative ἠμύσειε is ‘would’. ἠμύσειε is the aorist optative of ἠμύω ‘bow down, sink forward’ (not ἀμύνω ‘ward off’), and it is said of a city as ‘fall’. ἁλοῦσα is the aorist participle of ἁλίσκομαι ‘be taken’, and περθομένη the present passive participle of πέρθω ‘sack’, so the city is both captured and sacked. ὑφ’ ἡμετέρῃσιν is ὑπὸ ἡμετέρῃσιν, ‘beneath our (hands)’, with the epic dative plural feminine -ῃσιν agreeing with χερσίν. ἄνακτος is ‘lord’, the title of Priam.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά μοι αἰγίοχος Κρονίδης Ζεὺς ἄλγε’ ἔδωκεν,
ὅς με μετ’ ἀπρήκτους ἔριδας καὶ νείκεα βάλλει.
sentences.l:
But to me aegis-bearing Zeus, the son-of-Cronus, gave pains,
who among fruitless strifes and quarrels throws me.
sentences.i: But aegis-bearing Zeus, the son of Cronus, has given me pains: he casts me into the midst of fruitless strifes and quarrels.
sentences.n: ἀλλά sets his real situation against the wish. αἰγίοχος ‘aegis-bearing’ (sense disputed) and Κρονίδης ‘son of Cronus’ both belong to Ζεύς. ἄλγε’ is ἄλγεα ‘pains’, with the final vowel elided, and ἔδωκεν is the aorist of δίδωμι. ὅς is the relative, ‘who’; μετά with the accusative is ‘into the midst of’, and βάλλει is ‘throws’. ἀπρήκτους, from ἄπρηκτος ‘without result’, is the word of ‘a fruitless war’ at 2.121. ἔρις ‘strife’ and νεῖκος ‘quarrel’ stand together as a pair. Agamemnon blames Zeus, as he did at 2.111–112.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼν Ἀχιλεύς τε μαχεσσάμεθ’ εἵνεκα κούρης
ἀντιβίοις ἐπέεσσιν, ἐγὼ δ’ ἦρχον χαλεπαίνων·
sentences.l:
For indeed I and Achilles fought on account of a girl
with words of opposition, and I began it, growing harsh;
sentences.i: For I and Achilles fought over a girl with opposing words, and I was the one who began it, in my anger;
sentences.n: καὶ γάρ is ‘for indeed’, offering proof of the quarrels just named. μαχεσσάμεθ’ is the aorist of μάχομαι ‘fight’, and ἀντιβίοις ἐπέεσσιν ‘with words of opposition’ shows that this fight was in words; the phrase is the one at 1.304, with the shorter dative ending -οις. ἐγών is ἐγώ with a final ν. εἵνεκα κούρης is ‘on account of a girl’, Briseis (1.184), unnamed here. ἦρχον is ‘I began’, with the object, the quarrel, left to be understood, so Agamemnon admits that he started it. χαλεπαίνων is the participle of χαλεπαίνω, from χαλεπός ‘harsh’, ‘growing harsh, being fierce’; the English ‘in my anger’ gives the sense.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ ποτ’ ἔς γε μίαν βουλεύσομεν, οὐκέτ’ ἔπειτα
Τρωσὶν ἀνάβλησις κακοῦ ἔσσεται οὐδ’ ἠβαιόν.
sentences.l:
But if ever, to one (plan) at least, we shall take counsel, no longer then
for the Trojans will there be a putting-off of evil, not even a little.
sentences.i: But if ever we take counsel together for one plan, there will then be no more delay of evil for the Trojans, not the least bit.
sentences.n: εἰ δέ ποτε is ‘but if ever’, and the unnamed ‘we’ are Agamemnon and Achilles (377). ἔς γε μίαν has the feminine ‘one’ with no noun, and the noun to be supplied is ‘plan’ (βουλήν): to ‘take counsel to one (plan)’ is to agree. βουλεύσομεν can be read as a short-vowel aorist subjunctive (= βουλεύσωμεν) or as a future, and either gives ‘if ever we take counsel’. Τρωσίν is the dative plural of Τρῶες ‘Trojans’, ‘for the Trojans’. ἀνάβλησις ‘putting-off’ is a rare noun of ἀναβάλλω, and κακοῦ is the genitive, ‘of evil’, that is, of disaster. οὐδ’ ἠβαιόν, from ἠβαιός ‘little’, is adverbial: ‘not even a little’.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ ἔρχεσθ’ ἐπὶ δεῖπνον ἵνα ξυνάγωμεν Ἄρηα.
sentences.l: But now go to your meal, so that we may bring Ares together.
sentences.i: But now go to your meal, so that we may join battle.
sentences.n: νῦν δέ turns from reproach to orders. ἔρχεσθ’ is the plural imperative of ἔρχομαι, ἐπὶ δεῖπνον is ‘to the meal’, and ἵνα with the subjunctive ξυνάγωμεν is purpose. ξυνάγωμεν has the old spelling ξυν- for συν-, ‘bring together’. Ἄρηα is Ares, who stands for war itself, so ‘bring Ares together’ is the idiom for joining battle, here set in the English as ‘join battle’.

sentences.t:
εὖ μέν τις δόρυ θηξάσθω, εὖ δ’ ἀσπίδα θέσθω,
εὖ δέ τις ἵπποισιν δεῖπνον δότω ὠκυπόδεσσιν,
εὖ δέ τις ἅρματος ἀμφὶς ἰδὼν πολέμοιο μεδέσθω,
ὥς κε πανημέριοι στυγερῷ κρινώμεθ’ Ἄρηϊ.
sentences.l:
Well let each man whet his spear, well put his shield in order,
well let each man give his swift-footed horses a meal,
well let each, looking round his chariot, be mindful of war,
so that all day long we may be decided by hateful Ares.
sentences.i: Let each man whet his spear well and put his shield in good order, let each give his swift-footed horses their meal, and let each look well round his chariot and be mindful of war, so that we may fight it out all day long in hateful war.
sentences.n: Four commands, each opening with εὖ ‘well’ and each in the third person: θηξάσθω (θήγω ‘whet’, middle), θέσθω (τίθημι ‘put’, here ‘put in order’), δότω (δίδωμι) and μεδέσθω (μέδομαι ‘be mindful of’, with the genitive πολέμοιο). τις ‘someone’ is ‘each man’. ἀμφὶς ἰδών is ‘looking round’ the chariot, and ὠκυπόδεσσιν is the dative plural in -εσσι of ὠκύπους ‘swift-footed’. ὥς κε with the subjunctive κρινώμεθ’ is purpose; πανημέριοι is ‘all day long’; κρίνομαι ‘be decided’ is ‘be settled, fight it out’; and στυγερῷ Ἄρηϊ ‘hateful Ares’ is war, as at 381.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ παυσωλή γε μετέσσεται οὐδ’ ἠβαιὸν
εἰ μὴ νὺξ ἐλθοῦσα διακρινέει μένος ἀνδρῶν.
sentences.l:
For no respite will there be among us, not even a little,
unless night coming shall part the might of men.
sentences.i: For there will be no pause among us, not the least bit, unless night comes and parts the might of men.
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason for the preparations. παυσωλή ‘respite’ is a rare noun from παύω ‘stop’. μετέσσεται is the epic future of μέτειμι (μετά + εἰμί), ‘will be among (us)’, with the σ doubled. οὐδ’ ἠβαιόν is as at 380. εἰ μή is ‘unless’, ἐλθοῦσα the aorist participle ‘coming’, and διακρινέει the future of διακρίνω ‘part, separate’, with the epic uncontracted -εει (it comes from the κρίνω of 385). μένος ἀνδρῶν is ‘the might of the men’, the strength they fight with.

sentences.t:
ἱδρώσει μέν τευ τελαμὼν ἀμφὶ στήθεσφιν
ἀσπίδος ἀμφιβρότης, περὶ δ’ ἔγχεϊ χεῖρα καμεῖται·
sentences.l:
Will sweat, of someone, the strap about his chest
of the man-covering shield, and about the spear his hand will grow weary;
sentences.i: On some man’s chest the strap of his man-covering shield will be wet with sweat, and his hand will grow weary round his spear;
sentences.n: ἱδρώσει is the future of ἱδρόω ‘sweat’, and τευ is τινος ‘someone’s’. τελαμών is the strap that carried the shield on the chest, and ἀμφὶ στήθεσφιν is ‘about the chest’, with the old suffix -φιν in place of the dative. ἀσπίδος ἀμφιβρότης is ‘of the man-covering shield’: ἀμφιβρότης is the feminine genitive of ἀμφιβρότη ‘covering the man on both sides’, in agreement with ἀσπίδος. περὶ δ’ ἔγχεϊ is ‘about the spear’, with the dative ἔγχεϊ (= Attic ἔγχει), and καμεῖται is the future of κάμνω ‘grow weary’.

sentences.t: ἱδρώσει δέ τευ ἵππος ἐΰξοον ἅρμα τιταίνων.
sentences.l: and someone’s horse will sweat, straining at the well-polished chariot.
sentences.i: and some man’s horse will sweat as it strains at the well-polished chariot.
sentences.n: The sentence repeats the pattern of the one before: ἱδρώσει δέ τευ, ‘and someone’s … will sweat’. ἵππος is the horse of a chariot team, and ἅρμα is the chariot, a neuter singular. ἐΰξοον, ‘well-polished’, is usually taken as ἐΰ- ‘well’ with the root of ξέω ‘scrape smooth’. τιταίνων is the participle of τιταίνω ‘stretch, strain’, here the horse stretching to its pull.

sentences.t:
ὃν δέ κ’ ἐγὼν ἀπάνευθε μάχης ἐθέλοντα νοήσω
μιμνάζειν παρὰ νηυσὶ κορωνίσιν, οὔ οἱ ἔπειτα
ἄρκιον ἐσσεῖται φυγέειν κύνας ἠδ’ οἰωνούς.
sentences.l:
And whomever I shall perceive, apart from the battle, willing
to linger beside the curved ships — not for him then
assured will it be to escape the dogs and the birds.”
sentences.i: And whomever I see, away from the fighting, wanting to linger by the curved ships, for him there will be no assurance of escaping the dogs and the birds.”
sentences.n: ὃν δέ κ’ … νοήσω is a general relative, ‘whomever I perceive’, with κε and the aorist subjunctive. ἐθέλοντα takes the infinitive μιμνάζειν ‘to linger’, and ἀπάνευθε μάχης is ‘apart from the battle’. κορωνίσιν is ‘curved’, as the Odyssey says of ships. οὔ οἱ is ‘not for him’. ἄρκιον ‘sufficient, certain’ is the usual understanding: there will be no sure way for him. ἐσσεῖται is the epic future of εἰμί, and φυγέειν the epic infinitive of φεύγω. κύνας ἠδ’ οἰωνούς, ‘dogs and birds’, is the fate of the unburied dead at 1.4–5. The closing quotation mark ends Agamemnon’s speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, Ἀργεῖοι δὲ μέγ’ ἴαχον ὡς ὅτε κῦμα
ἀκτῇ ἐφ’ ὑψηλῇ, ὅτε κινήσῃ Νότος ἐλθών,
προβλῆτι σκοπέλῳ·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the Argives shouted loudly, as a wave does on a high headland when the South Wind has come and stirred it, on a jutting crag;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ ends Agamemnon’s speech, and the paragraph begins with the army’s roar. Ἀργεῖοι ‘Argives’ is one of the three names of the army, and ἴαχον is the aorist of ἰάχω ‘shout’. The comparison, ὡς ὅτε κῦμα … ‘as when a wave …’, has no verb of its own: it takes ἴαχον over, ‘as a wave (roars)’, and the English says ‘does’. ἀκτῇ ἐφ’ ὑψηλῇ is ‘on a high headland’, and κινήσῃ is the aorist subjunctive, ‘has stirred it’. Νότος is the South Wind. προβλῆτι σκοπέλῳ is ‘on a jutting crag’, προβλής being ‘thrust forward’, as of the Odyssey’s headlands.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ οὔ ποτε κύματα λείπει
παντοίων ἀνέμων, ὅτ’ ἂν ἔνθ’ ἢ ἔνθα γένωνται.
sentences.l:
and it the waves never leave
of winds of every kind, whenever they come here or there.
sentences.i: and the waves of winds of every kind never leave it, whenever they come this way or that.
sentences.n: τόν is the crag of the line before. κύματα is a neuter plural with a singular verb, λείπει, which is the regular Greek rule. παντοίων ἀνέμων is ‘of winds of every kind’ and depends on κύματα. ὅτ’ ἂν … γένωνται is a general clause: ‘whenever they come to be’, and the subject is most naturally the winds, though the waves are grammatically possible. ἔνθ’ ἢ ἔνθα is ‘here or there’, ‘this way or that’; the same sense as ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα at 462.

sentences.t:
ἀνστάντες δ’ ὀρέοντο κεδασθέντες κατὰ νῆας,
κάπνισσάν τε κατὰ κλισίας, καὶ δεῖπνον ἕλοντο.
sentences.l:
And rising up they hurried off, scattered along the ships,
and made smoke along the huts, and took their meal.
sentences.i: Then they stood up and hurried off, scattering among the ships, and set the smoke rising among the huts, and took their meal.
sentences.n: ἀνστάντες is ἀναστάντες with the middle vowel dropped, ‘having stood up’. ὀρέοντο is an epic form with the root of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’: ‘they hurried off, set out’. κεδασθέντες is the passive participle of κεδάννυμι ‘scatter’. κάπνισσαν, the aorist of καπνίζω, is ‘made smoke’, the smoke of the cooking fires. κατά with the accusative (νῆας, κλισίας) is ‘along, among’, and a κλισίη is a ‘hut’ beside a ship. δεῖπνον ἕλοντο, with the middle ἕλοντο, is ‘took their meal’.

sentences.t:
ἄλλος δ’ ἄλλῳ ἔρεζε θεῶν αἰειγενετάων
εὐχόμενος θάνατόν τε φυγεῖν καὶ μῶλον Ἄρηος.
sentences.l:
And one to one, and another to another, sacrificed, of the gods, the forever-born,
praying to escape death and the toil of Ares.
sentences.i: Each man sacrificed to a different one of the everlasting gods, praying to escape death and the toil of battle.
sentences.n: ἄλλος δ’ ἄλλῳ is ‘one to one, another to another’: each man sacrifices to his own god. θεῶν αἰειγενετάων is partitive, ‘of the forever-born gods’; αἰειγενετάων has the epic genitive plural -άων, and αἰειγενέτης is ‘forever-born, everlasting’. ἔρεζε is the imperfect of ῥέζω ‘sacrifice, offer’, with the dative of the god. εὐχόμενος ‘praying’ takes the infinitive φυγεῖν ‘to escape’. μῶλον Ἄρηος is ‘the toil of Ares’, and Ares stands for battle.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ βοῦν ἱέρευσε ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων
πίονα πενταέτηρον ὑπερμενέϊ Κρονίωνι,
sentences.l:
But he an ox sacrificed, lord of men, Agamemnon,
a fat one, five-year-old, to the exceeding-strong son of Cronus,
sentences.i: Agamemnon, lord of men, sacrificed a fat five-year-old ox to the son of Cronus, of surpassing strength,
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὃ is ‘but he’, with ὅ as a pronoun; ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων, ‘lord of men’, is the stock title. βοῦν ἱέρευσε is ‘sacrificed an ox’, with ἱερεύω ‘sacrifice’. πίονα is ‘fat’ and πενταέτηρον ‘five years old’ (πέντε + ἔτος). ὑπερμενέϊ is the dative of ὑπερμενής ‘exceeding-strong, of surpassing strength’, a stock epithet, and Κρονίων is ‘the son of Cronus’, Zeus. The sentence goes on to the next unit.

sentences.t:
κίκλησκεν δὲ γέροντας ἀριστῆας Παναχαιῶν,
Νέστορα μὲν πρώτιστα καὶ Ἰδομενῆα ἄνακτα,
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτ’ Αἴαντε δύω καὶ Τυδέος υἱόν,
ἕκτον δ’ αὖτ’ Ὀδυσῆα Διὶ μῆτιν ἀτάλαντον.
sentences.l:
and he summoned the elders, the best men of the Achaeans all together,
Nestor first of all, and lord Idomeneus,
and then the two Ajaxes and the son of Tydeus,
and as sixth, in turn, Odysseus, the equal of Zeus in cunning.
sentences.i: and he summoned the elders, the best men of all the Achaeans: first of all Nestor and lord Idomeneus, then the two Ajaxes and the son of Tydeus, and sixth Odysseus, the equal of Zeus in cunning.
sentences.n: κίκλησκεν is the imperfect of κικλήσκω, the reduplicated form of καλέω, ‘was summoning’. γέροντας ἀριστῆας Παναχαιῶν is ‘the elders, the best men of the Achaeans all together’, Παναχαιῶν being the genitive plural of Παναχαιοί. The names are accusatives: Νέστορα, Ἰδομενῆα ἄνακτα ‘lord Idomeneus’, Αἴαντε δύω (a dual: two men called Ajax), Τυδέος υἱόν ‘the son of Tydeus’ (Diomedes, unnamed), and Ὀδυσῆα. ἕκτον δ’ αὖτ’ is ‘and sixth, in turn’. Διὶ μῆτιν ἀτάλαντον is the line-end of 2.169, with ἀτάλαντον ‘equal in weight’ and μῆτιν ‘in cunning’ an accusative of respect, so the English is the same.

sentences.t: αὐτόματος δέ οἱ ἦλθε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος·
sentences.l: Of his own accord came to him, good at the war-cry, Menelaus;
sentences.i: Menelaus, good at the war-cry, came to him unbidden;
sentences.n: αὐτόματος ‘of his own accord’ is an adjective used where English has an adverb. οἱ is ‘to him’, that is, to Agamemnon, and ἦλθε is the aorist of ἔρχομαι. βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’ is the stock epithet of Menelaus. Menelaus is not on Agamemnon’s list, which stops at six; he comes uninvited, and the next line says why.

sentences.t: ᾔδεε γὰρ κατὰ θυμὸν ἀδελφεὸν ὡς ἐπονεῖτο.
sentences.l: for he knew in his heart his brother, how he was toiling.
sentences.i: for he knew in his heart how hard his brother was toiling.
sentences.n: ᾔδεε is the pluperfect of οἶδα, ‘he knew’, in the open epic form (Attic ᾔδει). κατὰ θυμόν is ‘in his heart’. ἀδελφεόν is the epic form of ἀδελφός ‘brother’. ὡς ἐπονεῖτο is an indirect question after ᾔδεε, ‘how he was toiling’, with the imperfect of πονέομαι ‘toil, labour’. γάρ gives the reason for his coming unasked.

sentences.t: βοῦν δὲ περιστήσαντο καὶ οὐλοχύτας ἀνέλοντο·
sentences.l: And the ox they stood around, and took up the barley-for-sprinkling;
sentences.i: They stood round the ox and took up the barley for sprinkling;
sentences.n: περιστήσαντο is the aorist middle of περιΐστημι, with the ox as object it is literally ‘they set the ox round (themselves)’, and the sense is that they ‘stood round the ox’. οὐλοχύτας are the grains of barley, from οὖλαι ‘whole barley’ and χέω ‘pour’, to be sprinkled over the victim; they are thrown forward at 421. ἀνέλοντο is the aorist middle of ἀναιρέομαι, ‘took up’.

sentences.t: τοῖσιν δ’ εὐχόμενος μετέφη κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.l: and among them, praying, spoke lord Agamemnon:
sentences.i: And lord Agamemnon, praying, spoke among them:
sentences.n: τοῖσιν is ‘among them’, the epic dative plural, and δ’ ties the line to the sacrifice. εὐχόμενος ‘praying’ announces that the next speech is a prayer. μετέφη is the aorist of μετάφημι, ‘spoke among’, and κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων is ‘lord Agamemnon’, as at 2.100.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ κύδιστε μέγιστε κελαινεφὲς αἰθέρι ναίων
μὴ πρὶν ἐπ’ ἠέλιον δῦναι καὶ ἐπὶ κνέφας ἐλθεῖν
πρίν με κατὰ πρηνὲς βαλέειν Πριάμοιο μέλαθρον
αἰθαλόεν, πρῆσαι δὲ πυρὸς δηΐοιο θύρετρα,
sentences.l:
“Zeus, most glorious, greatest, dark-clouded one, in the aether dwelling,
not before the sun go down and darkness come on
before I cast down headlong the roof of Priam,
soot-blackened, and burn with hostile fire its doors,
sentences.i: “Zeus, most glorious, greatest, you of the dark clouds, who dwell in the bright upper air: let the sun not go down, nor darkness come on, before I have thrown down Priam’s palace headlong, soot-blackened, and burned its doors with hostile fire,
sentences.n: Agamemnon’s prayer to Zeus is a string of infinitives, with no verb of asking: μὴ πρίν … δῦναι … ἐλθεῖν … πρὶν … βαλέειν means ‘not before the sun sets and darkness comes on, before I have thrown down’, and the English makes it a wish, ‘let the sun not go down’. Ζεῦ κύδιστε μέγιστε are vocatives, κελαινεφές ‘dark-clouded one’ is an epithet, and αἰθέρι ναίων is ‘dwelling in the upper air’, αἰθήρ being the bright upper sky. ἠέλιον and κνέφας are the accusative subjects of the infinitives, with ἐπί ‘upon’ in both. κατὰ … βαλέειν is tmesis, ‘throw down’, with πρηνές ‘headlong’. Πριάμοιο μέλαθρον is ‘the roof of Priam’; αἰθαλόεν is ‘soot-blackened’, πρῆσαι the aorist infinitive of πρήθω ‘burn’, πυρὸς δηΐοιο ‘with hostile fire’, and θύρετρα ‘doors’.

sentences.t:
Ἑκτόρεον δὲ χιτῶνα περὶ στήθεσσι δαΐξαι
χαλκῷ ῥωγαλέον·
sentences.l:
and Hector’s tunic about his chest to rend
with bronze, torn to tatters;
sentences.i: and torn Hector’s tunic to rags about his chest with bronze;
sentences.n: The wish goes on in the infinitive δαΐξαι ‘to rend’ (from δαΐζω), after πρῆσαι. Ἑκτόρεον is an adjective made from Hector’s name, ‘Hector’s’, agreeing with χιτῶνα ‘tunic’. περὶ στήθεσσι is ‘about his chest’, with the dative plural, and χαλκῷ is ‘with bronze’, the weapon. ῥωγαλέον is ‘torn’, from the root of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’. To rend the tunic on the chest is to kill the man in it.

sentences.t:
πολέες δ’ ἀμφ’ αὐτὸν ἑταῖροι
πρηνέες ἐν κονίῃσιν ὀδὰξ λαζοίατο γαῖαν.
sentences.l:
and many companions about him
headlong in the dust may take the earth with their teeth.”
sentences.i: and may many of his companions around him fall face down in the dust and bite the earth.”
sentences.n: πολέες is the epic form of πολλοί ‘many’, and ἀμφ’ αὐτόν is ‘around him’, around Hector. πρηνέες ‘headlong, face down’ is the plural of the πρηνές of 414. ἐν κονίῃσιν is ‘in the dust’, a dative plural. ὀδάξ is ‘with the teeth’, and λαζοίατο is the optative of λάζομαι ‘take’, with the ending -οίατο for -οιντο, so the wish continues: ‘may take the earth with their teeth’, the image of falling in battle. The closing quotation mark ends the prayer.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἄρα πώ οἱ ἐπεκραίαινε Κρονίων,
ἀλλ’ ὅ γε δέκτο μὲν ἱρά, πόνον δ’ ἀμέγαρτον ὄφελλεν.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, but not yet for him did the son of Cronus bring it to fulfilment,
but he accepted the sacrifices, and increased the unenviable toil.
sentences.i: So he spoke, but the son of Cronus did not yet fulfil it for him; he accepted the sacrifices, but made the dreadful toil grow.
sentences.n: Zeus takes the offering and does not grant the prayer. ὣς ἔφατ’ closes the prayer, and οὐδ’ ἄρα πώ is ‘and not yet at all’. ἐπεκραίαινε is the imperfect of ἐπικραιαίνω ‘bring to fulfilment’, with οἱ ‘for him’. δέκτο is the aorist of δέχομαι ‘receive’ with no augment, and ἱρά is ἱερά ‘sacrifices’. ὄφελλεν is the imperfect of ὀφέλλω ‘increase’, not ὀφείλω ‘ought’. ἀμέγαρτον, ‘unenviable’, is traditionally ‘not to be envied’, so ‘dreadful’, though the sense is uncertain; whose toil it is, the poet does not say.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ εὔξαντο καὶ οὐλοχύτας προβάλοντο,
αὐέρυσαν μὲν πρῶτα καὶ ἔσφαξαν καὶ ἔδειραν,
μηρούς τ’ ἐξέταμον κατά τε κνίσῃ ἐκάλυψαν
δίπτυχα ποιήσαντες, ἐπ’ αὐτῶν δ’ ὠμοθέτησαν.
sentences.l:
But when they had prayed and had thrown forward the barley-for-sprinkling,
they drew back first, and slaughtered, and flayed,
the thighs they cut out and covered them over with fat,
making it double-folded, and on them they laid raw pieces;
sentences.i: When they had prayed and thrown down the barley for sprinkling, they first drew the victims’ heads back, slaughtered and flayed them, cut out the thighs, covered them with fat folded double, and laid raw morsels on them;
sentences.n: These are the four lines of 1.458–461, word for word, and the English is the same. The barley (410) is thrown forward, and the sacrifice goes through its usual stages. αὐέρυσαν ‘drew back’ has no object in the Greek: the heads of the victims are what is understood, and the English supplies them. ἔσφαξαν is ‘slaughtered’ and ἔδειραν ‘flayed’. The thighs (μηρούς) are wrapped in κνίσῃ, here the fat, not the ‘savour’ that rose at 1.317. δίπτυχα is ‘folded double’, and ὠμοθέτησαν ‘laid raw pieces’ on top of the thighs.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὰ μὲν ἂρ σχίζῃσιν ἀφύλλοισιν κατέκαιον,
σπλάγχνα δ’ ἄρ’ ἀμπείραντες ὑπείρεχον Ἡφαίστοιο.
sentences.l:
And these then on leafless split wood they burned up,
and the entrails, having spitted them, they held over Hephaestus.
sentences.i: These they burned on leafless split wood, and they spitted the entrails and held them over the flame of Hephaestus.
sentences.n: τὰ μέν … σπλάγχνα δέ sets the thighs against the entrails. σχίζῃσιν ἀφύλλοισιν is the dative ‘on leafless pieces of split wood’, and κατέκαιον the imperfect of κατακαίω ‘burn up’. ἀμπείραντες is ἀναπείραντες (ἀναπείρω ‘run through, spit’) with the vowel dropped and ν turned to μ before π. ὑπείρεχον is ὑπερεῖχον ‘held above’, and Ἡφαίστοιο is a genitive: Hephaestus, the god of the forge, stands for fire, as Ares for war. The English ‘flame’ makes that plain.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ κατὰ μῆρε κάη καὶ σπλάγχνα πάσαντο,
μίστυλλόν τ’ ἄρα τἆλλα καὶ ἀμφ’ ὀβελοῖσιν ἔπειραν,
ὤπτησάν τε περιφραδέως, ἐρύσαντό τε πάντα.
sentences.l:
But when the thigh-pieces were burned up and they had tasted the entrails,
they cut up the rest then into pieces and pierced them around spits,
and roasted them very carefully and drew them all off.
sentences.i: When the thigh-pieces were burned up and they had tasted the entrails, they cut up the rest into small pieces, pierced them on spits, roasted them with great care, and drew them all off.
sentences.n: The thighs are burned and the meal is made from the rest; the lines are the same as 1.464–466, and the English is the same. μῆρε, as the edition prints it, looks like a dual (‘the pair of thighs’), where the Odyssey has the plural μῆρ’, and the sense is the same. κάη is the aorist passive of καίω with no augment, with its preverb apart in κατὰ … κάη (tmesis). σπλάγχνα πάσαντο is ‘they tasted the entrails’. μίστυλλον and ἔπειραν are ‘cut into pieces’ and ‘pierced’, ἀμφ’ ὀβελοῖσιν ‘around spits’; ἐρύσαντο is ‘drew off’ the roasted meat, and περιφραδέως ‘with great care’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ παύσαντο πόνου τετύκοντό τε δαῖτα
δαίνυντ’, οὐδέ τι θυμὸς ἐδεύετο δαιτὸς ἐΐσης.
sentences.l:
And when they had ceased from toil and had made ready the feast,
they feasted, and not at all did the heart lack the equal feast.
sentences.i: And when they had ended their labour and prepared the meal, they feasted, and their hearts went short of nothing in the equally shared feast.
sentences.n: The meal itself. The lines are the same as 1.467–468, and the English is the same. παύσαντο πόνου is ‘ceased from toil’, with the genitive, and τετύκοντο is a reduplicated aorist of τεύχω ‘make ready’. δαίνυντ’ is δαίνυντο ‘they feasted’, an imperfect with no augment, and it follows the first half at once with no connecting word. ἐδεύετο ‘lacked’ takes the genitive δαιτὸς ἐΐσης ‘the equal feast’, ‘the equally shared feast’; θυμός ‘heart’ is the seat of appetite.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο,
τοῖς ἄρα μύθων ἦρχε Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ·
sentences.l:
But when of drink and of food they had put away desire,
among them then of speeches made-beginning the Gerenian horseman Nestor:
sentences.i: But when they had put from them the desire for drink and food, the Gerenian horseman Nestor was the first to speak among them:
sentences.n: The first line, which ends a meal, is the one shared with the Odyssey and found at 1.469, and the second is the Odyssey’s (3.68), so the English is the Odyssey’s. ἐξ … ἕντο is tmesis of ἐξίημι ‘put away’, with ἔρον ‘desire’ as the object, and πόσιος and ἐδητύος ‘of drink and food’ depend on it. τοῖς is ‘among them’, and μύθων ἦρχε is ‘began the speaking’, ‘was the first to speak’. Γερήνιος, Nestor’s stock epithet, is of uncertain meaning (Gerenia in Messenia is the usual guess), and ἱππότα ‘horseman’ is a nominative in short -α.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη κύδιστε ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγάμεμνον,
μηκέτι νῦν δήθ’ αὖθι λεγώμεθα, μηδ’ ἔτι δηρὸν
ἀμβαλλώμεθα ἔργον ὃ δὴ θεὸς ἐγγυαλίζει.
sentences.l:
“Atreus’-son, most glorious, lord of men, Agamemnon,
no longer now for long here let us talk, nor still for long
let us put off the work which indeed a god is placing in our hands.
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, most glorious Agamemnon, lord of men, let us talk here no longer, nor put off for long the work that a god is now putting into our hands.
sentences.n: Nestor’s advice is to stop talking and act. Ἀτρεΐδη κύδιστε ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγάμεμνον are four vocatives, and the Odyssey has the same line (11.397). μηκέτι νῦν is ‘no longer now’, δήθ’ is δήθα ‘for long’, and αὖθι is ‘here, on the spot’. λεγώμεθα is a hortatory subjunctive of λέγομαι; the usual understanding is ‘talk’, but the sense is not certain, and the English takes ‘talk’. ἀμβαλλώμεθα is ἀναβάλλομαι ‘put off’, with ἀν- changed to ἀμ- before β, and δηρόν is ‘for a long time’. ἐγγυαλίζει is ‘puts into the hands’, and the god is not named.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε κήρυκες μὲν Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων
λαὸν κηρύσσοντες ἀγειρόντων κατὰ νῆας,
ἡμεῖς δ’ ἀθρόοι ὧδε κατὰ στρατὸν εὐρὺν Ἀχαιῶν
ἴομεν ὄφρα κε θᾶσσον ἐγείρομεν ὀξὺν Ἄρηα.
sentences.l:
But come, let the heralds of the bronze-shirted Achaeans,
summoning the people, gather them along the ships,
and let us, all together, thus through the wide army of the Achaeans
go, so that the more quickly we may rouse sharp Ares.”
sentences.i: But come, let the heralds of the bronze-shirted Achaeans summon the people and gather them along the ships, and let us go all together in this way through the wide army of the Achaeans, so that we may the sooner rouse keen battle.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’, and the proposal has two parts, the heralds’ and the chiefs’. ἀγειρόντων is the third person plural imperative of ἀγείρω ‘gather’, and κηρύσσοντες λαόν is ‘summoning the people’; ἀγείρω is not the ἐγείρω ‘rouse’ of 440. ἡμεῖς δ’ ἀθρόοι is ‘and we all together’, and ὧδε is ‘in this way’. ἴομεν is a short-vowel hortatory subjunctive of εἶμι, ‘let us go’. ὄφρα κε with the subjunctive ἐγείρομεν is purpose, and θᾶσσον is the comparative of ταχύς, ‘the sooner’. ὀξὺν Ἄρηα is ‘sharp Ares’, and Ares stands for battle. The closing quotation mark ends Nestor’s speech.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and did not disobey, the lord of men, Agamemnon.
sentences.i: So Nestor spoke, and Agamemnon, lord of men, did not disobey.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ closes Nestor’s speech, and the paragraph begins. οὐδ’ ἀπίθησεν is ‘and did not disobey’, the verb of 1.220, where Achilles obeyed Athena; ἀπιθέω is the opposite of πείθομαι ‘obey’. The subject is held to the end of the line, ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων ‘Agamemnon, lord of men’, the stock title.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα κηρύκεσσι λιγυφθόγγοισι κέλευσε
κηρύσσειν πόλεμον δὲ κάρη κομόωντας Ἀχαιούς·
sentences.l:
At once to the clear-voiced heralds he gave-command
to summon to war the long-haired-of-head Achaeans;
sentences.i: At once he ordered the clear-voiced heralds to summon the long-haired Achaeans to war;
sentences.n: The lines are those of 2.50–51 with αὐτίκα ‘at once’ for αὐτὰρ ὃ ‘but he’ and πόλεμον δέ ‘to war’ for ἀγορὴν δέ ‘to assembly’, and the English follows the earlier unit. κηρύκεσσι λιγυφθόγγοισι is the dative ‘to the clear-voiced heralds’, with the epic endings -εσσι and -οισι, and κέλευσε ‘ordered’ takes the infinitive κηρύσσειν ‘to summon’. πόλεμον δέ is πόλεμόνδε ‘to war’, with δέ as the suffix of direction, printed as two words. κάρη κομόωντας is ‘long-haired’, an accusative of respect (‘with respect to the head’), and the line has a stop after Ἀχαιούς.

sentences.t: οἳ μὲν ἐκήρυσσον, τοὶ δ’ ἠγείροντο μάλ’ ὦκα.
sentences.l: They made-proclamation, and the others gathered very quickly;
sentences.i: The heralds made the proclamation, and the people gathered very quickly;
sentences.n: οἳ μὲν … τοὶ δ’ is ‘these … those’, the article used as a pronoun: the heralds and the people. The line is the same as 2.52, and the English is the same. ἐκήρυσσον is the imperfect, ‘kept proclaiming’, and ἠγείροντο the imperfect passive of ἐγείρω, ‘were roused, gathered’. μάλ’ ὦκα is ‘very quickly’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἀμφ’ Ἀτρεΐωνα διοτρεφέες βασιλῆες
θῦνον κρίνοντες,
sentences.l:
And they, about Atreus’-son, the Zeus-nurtured kings,
rushed about, sorting them,
sentences.i: And the Zeus-nurtured kings hurried about the son of Atreus, sorting them,
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ is ‘and they’, and the kings are named in apposition: διοτρεφέες βασιλῆες ‘Zeus-nurtured kings’ is a stock phrase. ἀμφ’ Ἀτρεΐωνα is ‘about the son of Atreus’ (Agamemnon), and θῦνον is the imperfect of θύνω ‘rush’. κρίνοντες is the participle of κρίνω ‘sort’; the Greek gives no object, and the English supplies ‘them’, the army, since sorting the men is what Nestor advised at 362.

sentences.t:
μετὰ δὲ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη
αἰγίδ’ ἔχουσ’ ἐρίτιμον ἀγήρων ἀθανάτην τε,
τῆς ἑκατὸν θύσανοι παγχρύσεοι ἠερέθονται,
πάντες ἐϋπλεκέες, ἑκατόμβοιος δὲ ἕκαστος·
sentences.l:
and among them gleaming-eyed Athena,
holding the aegis, much-honoured, ageless, and immortal,
of which a hundred tassels, all-golden, hang waving,
all well-plaited, and each one worth a hundred oxen;
sentences.i: and among them was gleaming-eyed Athena, holding the aegis, much honoured, ageless and immortal, from which a hundred tassels, all of gold, hang waving, every one finely plaited, and each worth a hundred oxen;
sentences.n: μετὰ δέ is the adverb ‘and among (them)’, Athena’s verb is διέσσυτο at 450, after the picture of the aegis, and the English supplies ‘was’ to carry that picture. γλαυκῶπις ‘gleaming-eyed’ is Athena’s stock epithet. αἰγίδ’ ἔχουσ’ is ‘holding the aegis’, her shield-cape, with the elided αἰγίδα. ἐρίτιμον ‘much-honoured’ has the intensive ἐρι-, and ἀγήρων is ‘ageless’. τῆς is ‘of which’, the aegis, and θύσανοι are ‘tassels’; παγχρύσεοι is ‘all of gold’, and ἠερέθονται, from a rare verb, is ‘hang waving’. πάντες ἐϋπλεκέες is ‘all well-plaited’, and ἑκατόμβοιος is ‘worth a hundred oxen’ (ἑκατόν + βοῦς).

sentences.t:
σὺν τῇ παιφάσσουσα διέσσυτο λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν
ὀτρύνουσ’ ἰέναι·
sentences.l:
With it, darting about, she rushed through the people of the Achaeans,
urging them to go;
sentences.i: With it she darted about and rushed through the army of the Achaeans, urging them forward;
sentences.n: σὺν τῇ is ‘with it’, the aegis. παιφάσσουσα is a participle of the rare verb παιφάσσω, ‘darting about’ being the usual understanding. διέσσυτο is the aorist middle of διασεύω ‘rush through’, with λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν ‘the people of the Achaeans’. ὀτρύνουσ’ is ὀτρύνουσα, ‘urging’, and ἰέναι is the infinitive of εἶμι, ‘to go’. The unit ends in the middle of line 451, at the edition’s ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ σθένος ὦρσεν ἑκάστῳ
καρδίῃ ἄλληκτον πολεμίζειν ἠδὲ μάχεσθαι.
sentences.l:
and in each man she roused strength, in his heart,
unceasing, to wage war and to fight.
sentences.i: and she roused in the heart of each man unceasing strength to wage war and to fight.
sentences.n: ἐν … ὦρσεν is tmesis, ‘roused in’ (the aorist of ὄρνυμι), with σθένος ‘strength’. ἑκάστῳ καρδίῃ is ‘in each man’s heart’, a dative of the person and a dative of place together. ἄλληκτον ‘unceasing’ comes from α- ‘not’ and λήγω ‘stop’, and πολεμίζειν ἠδὲ μάχεσθαι is ‘to wage war and to fight’, two infinitives. The unit begins in the middle of line 451.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ ἄφαρ πόλεμος γλυκίων γένετ’ ἠὲ νέεσθαι
ἐν νηυσὶ γλαφυρῇσι φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν.
sentences.l:
And to them straightway war became sweeter than to go back
in the hollow ships to their dear fatherland.
sentences.i: And at once war became sweeter to them than going home in their hollow ships to their dear fatherland.
sentences.n: τοῖσι δ’ is ‘and to them’, the Achaeans, and ἄφαρ is ‘at once’. γλυκίων is the comparative of γλυκύς ‘sweeter’, with ἠέ ‘than’ and the infinitive νέεσθαι ‘to go back’. ἐν νηυσὶ γλαφυρῇσι is ‘in the hollow ships’, with the epic datives -υσι and -ῃσι, and φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν is ‘to their dear fatherland’. The line undoes the rush to the ships of 2.149–154.

sentences.t:
ἠΰτε πῦρ ἀΐδηλον ἐπιφλέγει ἄσπετον ὕλην
οὔρεος ἐν κορυφῇς, ἕκαθεν δέ τε φαίνεται αὐγή,
ὣς τῶν ἐρχομένων ἀπὸ χαλκοῦ θεσπεσίοιο
αἴγλη παμφανόωσα δι’ αἰθέρος οὐρανὸν ἷκε.
sentences.l:
As a destroying fire blazes over boundless forest
on the peaks of a mountain, and from afar its glare is seen,
so of them as they went, from the wondrous bronze,
the all-shining gleam through the upper air reached heaven.
sentences.i: As a destructive fire blazes over boundless forest on the peaks of a mountain, and its glare is seen from far off, so from the wondrous bronze of the men as they marched an all-shining gleam went up through the upper air and reached heaven.
sentences.n: ἠΰτε is ‘as, like’ and begins the simile that answers with ὣς at 457. πῦρ ἀΐδηλον is ‘destroying fire’; ἀΐδηλος means either ‘destroying’ or ‘unseen’, and the English takes the first. ἐπιφλέγει is ‘blazes over’, with ἄσπετον ὕλην ‘boundless forest’. οὔρεος is the epic genitive of ὄρος, and κορυφῇς an epic dative plural, ‘on the peaks’. ἕκαθεν is ‘from afar’, and φαίνεται ‘is seen’. In ὣς τῶν ἐρχομένων, ‘so of them as they went’, the genitive goes with ἀπὸ χαλκοῦ θεσπεσίοιο ‘from the wondrous bronze’, their armour. αἴγλη παμφανόωσα is ‘an all-shining gleam’, and ἷκε is the aorist ‘reached’ with no augment.

sentences.t:
τῶν δ’ ὥς τ’ ὀρνίθων πετεηνῶν ἔθνεα πολλὰ
χηνῶν ἢ γεράνων ἢ κύκνων δουλιχοδείρων
Ἀσίω ἐν λειμῶνι Καϋστρίου ἀμφὶ ῥέεθρα
ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα ποτῶνται ἀγαλλόμενα πτερύγεσσι
κλαγγηδὸν προκαθιζόντων, σμαραγεῖ δέ τε λειμών,
sentences.l:
And of them, as of winged birds the many tribes,
of geese or of cranes or of long-necked swans,
in the Asian meadow about the streams of the Cayster
here and there fly about, exulting in their wings,
settling down ahead with clamour, and the meadow resounds,
sentences.i: And as the many swarms of winged birds, of geese or of cranes or of long-necked swans, fly about this way and that in the Asian meadow around the streams of the Cayster, exulting in their wings and settling down ahead with clamour, and the meadow resounds,
sentences.n: A second simile, this time of birds, whose verb comes only in the third line. τῶν δ’ is ‘and of them’, the marching army; it looks ahead to the τῶν of 464, where the comparison is finished, and the English leaves it out. ὥς τε is ‘just as’, and ἔθνεα is ‘tribes’ in the literal layer and ‘swarms’ in the English, as at 464. The kinds are χηνῶν ‘geese’, γεράνων ‘cranes’ and κύκνων δουλιχοδείρων ‘long-necked swans’, all genitive plurals. The verb is ποτῶνται, from ποτάομαι ‘fly about’, with ἔθνεα as subject. Ἀσίω (the dative, usually written Ἀσίῳ) is ‘Asian’: the meadow lies by the Cayster (Καϋστρίου) in Asia Minor. ἀγαλλόμενα ‘exulting’ agrees with ἔθνεα; προκαθιζόντων, a genitive plural participle, ‘settling down ahead’, agrees with ὀρνίθων; σμαραγεῖ is ‘resounds’.

sentences.t:
ὣς τῶν ἔθνεα πολλὰ νεῶν ἄπο καὶ κλισιάων
ἐς πεδίον προχέοντο Σκαμάνδριον·
sentences.l:
so of them the many tribes, from the ships and the huts,
poured forth into the Scamandrian plain;
sentences.i: so their many swarms, from the ships and the huts, poured out onto the Scamandrian plain;
sentences.n: ὣς τῶν finishes the comparison: ‘so of them’. The first line is the one at 2.91, and the English follows the earlier unit; ἔθνεα picks up the word of 459, now for companies of soldiers. νεῶν ἄπο is ἀπὸ νεῶν, with the preposition after its noun, and κλισιάων is the epic genitive plural of κλισίη ‘hut’. ἐς πεδίον is ‘into the plain’, and προχέοντο is the imperfect middle of προχέω, ‘poured forth’. Σκαμάνδριον is the adjective of the Scamander, the river of Troy. The unit ends in the middle of line 465, at the edition’s ano teleia.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὑπὸ χθὼν
σμερδαλέον κονάβιζε ποδῶν αὐτῶν τε καὶ ἵππων.
sentences.l:
but beneath, the earth
frightfully rang with the feet of the men themselves and of horses.
sentences.i: but the earth beneath them rang frightfully with the feet of the men themselves and of the horses.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 465. ὑπὸ … χθών, ‘the earth beneath’, has ὑπό apart from its noun. σμερδαλέον is the neuter accusative of σμερδαλέος ‘frightful’ used as an adverb, and κονάβιζε is the imperfect of κοναβίζω ‘resound, ring’. ποδῶν is the genitive of cause, ‘with the feet’, and αὐτῶν τε καὶ ἵππων is ‘of the men themselves and of horses’: αὐτῶν ‘themselves’ means the men on foot, set against the horses.

sentences.t:
ἔσταν δ’ ἐν λειμῶνι Σκαμανδρίῳ ἀνθεμόεντι
μυρίοι, ὅσσά τε φύλλα καὶ ἄνθεα γίγνεται ὥρῃ.
sentences.l:
And they stood in the Scamandrian meadow, flowery,
countless, as many as leaves and flowers that come in their season.
sentences.i: They took their stand in the flowery meadow of the Scamander, countless as the leaves and flowers that come in their season.
sentences.n: ἔσταν is ἔστησαν, the aorist of ἵστημι in the intransitive sense, ‘took their stand’, with the epic ending -αν. ἐν λειμῶνι Σκαμανδρίῳ ἀνθεμόεντι is ‘in the flowery Scamandrian meadow’, ἀνθεμόεις ‘flowery’ being from ἄνθεμον ‘blossom’, and the meadow echoes the Cayster meadow of the simile. μυρίοι is ‘countless’, literally ten thousand. ὅσσα τε is ‘as many as’, with no ὡς, so the comparison sits in the relative clause. φύλλα καὶ ἄνθεα are ‘leaves and flowers’, and γίγνεται is a singular verb with a neuter plural subject. ὥρῃ is the dative of time, ‘in season’.
